name: Lingala
confidence_why: The penultimate-stress record rests on one aside in Redden & Bongo 1963, a teaching course that itself calls Lingala a two-tone language and attributes penultimate stress only to some speakers who do not use tone, while Meeuwis 2013 and Meeuwis 2019 describe lexical and grammatical tone with minimal pairs and no word stress at all.
catalog_quote: there are many speakers of Lingala who use a stress system instead of tones. Most speakers who use a stress system stress the penultimate syllable.

audit.recode_to: tonal (H/L lexical and grammatical tone), with a caution note that some L2/urban speakers replace tone with penultimate stress (Redden & Bongo 1963: xi); if the catalog keeps a stress entry it should be 'conflict'/'variable', not 'fixed-strict' with in the dominant set — confirm against Meeuwis 2020 phonology chapter before finalising.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on printed p. xi of the FSI PDF we hold (PDF p. 12), and the record is a StressTyp2 coding whose StressTyp2 reference is exactly Redden & Bongo 1963. (2) But the source is a 1963 pedagogical course, and the quoted sentence is embedded in a passage that says Lingala 'is a tone language', has 'two contrastive or phonemic tones', and that 'the majority of speakers of the language do use tone, including the speaker used as the model for this manual'; penultimate stress is attributed only to the subset of speakers 'who use a stress system instead of tones'. Coding the language as fixed-strict penultimate with in the dominant set therefore over-reads the source. (3) The held modern description by the language's principal describer (Meeuwis 2013, APiCS ch. 60 and structure dataset) gives lexically and grammatically distinctive H/L tone with minimal pairs and no wo

sources.quote: "Contrast between low tones ... and high tones ... is lexically and grammatically distinctive" with minimal pairs (ngámbo/ngambo, kokóma/kokoma, sángó/sango; nápésa vs napésá); APiCS feature 120 value: 'Simple tone system, for lexical and grammatical distinctions'. No word-stress statement anywhere in the chapter (only 'contrastive stress' = focus on a head noun).
